solution:
Let x : (p Δ q) ⇒ (pΔ ~ q) ∨ (~ p Δq) 
Case-I 
When Δ is same as ∨ 
Then (p Δ ~ q) ∨ (~ p Δ q) becomes 
(p ∨ ~ q) ∨ (~ p ∨ q) which is always true, so x becomes a tautology. 
Case-II 
When Δ is same as ∧ 
Then (p ∧ q) ⇒ (p∧ ~ q) ∨ (~ p ∧ q) 
If p ∧ q is T, then (p ∧ ~ q) ∨ (~ p ∧ q) is F so x cannot be a tautology. 
Case-III 
When Δ is same as ⇒ 
Then (p ⇒ ~ q) ∨ (~ p ⇒ q) is same at (~ p ∨ ~ q) ∨ (p ∨ q), which is always true, so x becomes a tautology. 
Case-IV 
When Δ is same as ⇔ 
Then (p ⇔ q) ⇒ (p ⇔ ~ q) ∨ (~ p ⇔ q) 
p ⇔ q is true when p and q have same truth values, then p ⇔ ~ q and ~p ⇔ q both are false. Hence x cannot
